lessons.title: Scheduling and Calendar Management
lessons.body: As a DJ, your calendar is your lifeline. Double-booking a gig means losing money and damaging your reputation. Start by using a digital calendar like Google Calendar or a paper diary if you prefer. Sync it across your phone and laptop so you always have it. For each booking, record the date, time, venue, client name, contact number, and fee. Also block out travel time, setup and breakdown times, and rest days. In Africa, traffic and distances can be unpredictable, so add a 30% buffer to travel estimates. For example, if a venue is 1 hour away, block 1.5 hours. Use colour coding: red for confirmed gigs, yellow for pending, blue for personal. Set reminders: one week before, one day before, and two hours before. Always confirm with the client 48 hours prior. If you get a new inquiry for a date you're already booked, offer a backup DJ from your network or ask if the date is flexible. Keep a waiting list. At the end of each month, review your calendar to see your busiest days and plan marketing accordingly. Also, schedule time for admin, equipment maintenance, and practice. A well-managed calendar reduces stress and helps you say yes to the right gigs.

lessons.title: Client Communication and Follow-Up
lessons.body: Clear communication is the difference between a happy client and a nightmare. When a client first contacts you, respond within 24 hours. Use WhatsApp or email, whichever they prefer. Ask key questions: event type, date, time, venue, number of guests, music preferences, and budget. Send a written quote within 48 hours. The quote should list your fee, deposit (usually 50%), and what's included (e.g., sound system, lights, MC services). Once they agree, send a simple contract or confirmation message outlining the details. Two weeks before the event, have a planning call to finalise the playlist, announcements, and timeline. One week before, send a reminder of the deposit balance and arrival time. After the event, follow up within 48 hours with a thank-you message and a request for a testimonial. Offer a discount for referrals. Keep a client database (Google Sheets or a notebook) with names, contacts, event dates, and preferences. If a client complains, listen, apologise, and offer a solution. For example, if the music was too loud, offer a free hour at their next event. Good follow-up leads to repeat bookings and word-of-mouth referrals, which are crucial in the African market where trust is key.

lessons.title: Managing Subcontractors and Assistants
lessons.body: As your business grows, you'll need help. Subcontractors can be other DJs, MCs, sound engineers, or lighting technicians. Assistants can handle setup, carry equipment, or manage requests. Start by building a list of reliable people. Test them on small gigs before trusting them with big ones. When you hire a subcontractor, agree on a fixed fee or percentage (e.g., 60% to you, 40% to them) and put it in writing. For assistants, pay a daily rate: in many African cities, $20-$50 per event is common. Always brief them at least 3 days before: share the event schedule, playlist, and dress code. On the day, arrive together or meet at the venue. Assign clear roles: one person manages the mixer, another handles requests. Have a backup plan if someone cancels last minuteâkeep 2-3 standby contacts. Pay promptly after the event; late payment ruins relationships. Also, treat them with respect: provide water and food, and credit them in your social media posts. If a subcontractor does well, book them again and consider a retainer for regular gigs. Remember, your reputation depends on their performance, so invest time in training and clear communication.

lessons.title: Equipment Maintenance and Inventory
lessons.body: Your equipment is your livelihood. Without it, you can't perform. Keep an inventory list (use Google Sheets or a notebook) with every item: speakers, mixer, laptop, headphones, microphones, cables, lights, and stands. Record purchase date, cost, and serial numbers. After every gig, inspect equipment for damage. Clean speakers with a dry cloth, check cables for frays, and test microphones. Store everything in a dry, secure placeâhumidity and dust are enemies. In Africa, power surges are common, so use a surge protector and a voltage stabiliser. For generators, keep fuel fresh and change oil every 50 hours. Create a maintenance schedule: monthly check all cables, quarterly clean mixer faders, annually service speakers. Keep a small repair kit with spare fuses, soldering iron, and duct tape. If something breaks, fix it immediately or have a backup. For example, always carry a spare microphone and a backup laptop. Track when items need replacement: cables last about 2 years, speakers 5-7 years. Insurance is rare in many African markets, so self-insure by setting aside 10% of each gig fee for repairs. Also, label everything with your name and phone number to prevent theft or loss.

lessons.title: Travel and Logistics for Mobile DJs
lessons.body: Mobile DJs in Africa face unique travel challenges: bad roads, traffic jams, and long distances. Plan your route using Google Maps or local knowledge. For a gig 100km away, leave at least 3 hours early. If you don't have a vehicle, hire a taxi or vanâbudget $50-$100 for local trips. For longer trips, consider a bus or train, but pack equipment in sturdy cases. Always carry equipment yourself; never check it in as luggage. Have a checklist: speakers, mixer, laptop, cables, lights, stands, extension cords, and backup power (inverter or generator). Arrive at least 2 hours before start time to set up. If you're staying overnight, book accommodation near the venue and confirm parking security. Keep a copy of your booking confirmation and venue contact on your phone. For international gigs, check visa requirements and customs rules for equipment. In some countries, you need a carnet for professional equipment. Also, pack a small emergency kit: water, snacks, painkillers, and a change of clothes. After the event, pack down efficiently and secure everything. If you're too tired to drive, sleep before returning. Always inform someone of your travel plans. Good logistics mean you arrive relaxed and ready to perform.

lessons.title: Crisis Management and Backup Plans
lessons.body: Even with the best planning, crises happen. Power cuts, equipment failure, sudden rain, or a client who changes the schedule last minute. Your job is to stay calm and have a backup plan. For power cuts, carry a generator or inverter. Test it before the event. For equipment failure, have spares: a second laptop, extra cables, and a backup mixer. If your main speakers blow, use a smaller backup set or rent from a local contact. Keep a list of emergency contacts: a sound engineer, a rental shop, and a fellow DJ. For rain, have tarpaulins or move under cover. If the client is unhappy, listen and offer alternativesâmaybe a different genre or a short break. If you're sick, have a trusted DJ on standby who can cover for you. Always have a written agreement with a cancellation policy: if you cancel, you refund the deposit; if the client cancels, you keep the deposit. For lost or stolen equipment, file a police report and claim insurance if you have it. After any crisis, review what went wrong and update your plan. Practice crisis drills: simulate a power cut and see how fast you can switch to backup. The key is to never panic in front of the client. Your confidence reassures them and saves the event.

quiz.q: What is the recommended buffer time for travel when scheduling a gig?
quiz.explanation: A 30% buffer accounts for unpredictable traffic and distances in Africa.

quiz.q: How far in advance should you confirm with a client before an event?
quiz.explanation: Confirming 48 hours prior ensures details are fresh and reduces no-shows.

quiz.q: Which tool is recommended for keeping a digital calendar?
quiz.explanation: Google Calendar syncs across devices and allows reminders and colour coding.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get a new inquiry for a date you're already booked?
quiz.explanation: Offering a backup DJ maintains goodwill and may lead to future bookings.

quiz.q: How often should you review your calendar for planning?
quiz.explanation: Monthly reviews help identify busy periods and plan marketing.

quiz.q: What is the recommended deposit percentage for a DJ booking?
quiz.explanation: A 50% deposit secures the date and covers initial costs.

quiz.q: How soon should you respond to a new client inquiry?
quiz.explanation: Responding within 24 hours shows professionalism and increases conversion.

quiz.q: What should you send to a client after agreeing on details?
options: B) A written contract or confirmation
D) A invoice for full payment
quiz.explanation: A written contract or confirmation outlines expectations and protects both parties.

quiz.q: When should you have a planning call with the client?
quiz.explanation: A call two weeks prior allows time to finalise playlist and timeline.

quiz.q: What is a good way to get more bookings from a satisfied client?
options: A) Ask for a testimonial and offer referral discount
quiz.explanation: Testimonials and referral discounts encourage repeat and word-of-mouth business.

quiz.q: What percentage split is suggested for a subcontractor DJ?
quiz.explanation: A 60/40 split (you/subcontractor) is a common fair arrangement.

quiz.q: How much is a typical daily rate for an assistant in many African cities?
quiz.explanation: $20-$50 per event is a reasonable rate for assistants in many African markets.

quiz.q: How many days before an event should you brief your subcontractors?
quiz.explanation: Briefing 3 days before gives them time to prepare and ask questions.

quiz.q: What should you do if a subcontractor cancels last minute?
quiz.explanation: Keeping standby contacts ensures you can cover last-minute cancellations.

quiz.q: Why is it important to pay subcontractors promptly?
quiz.explanation: Prompt payment builds trust and ensures they will work with you again.

quiz.q: What should you use to protect equipment from power surges?
quiz.explanation: A surge protector shields equipment from voltage spikes common in Africa.

quiz.q: How often should you check all cables for damage?
quiz.explanation: Monthly checks catch wear and tear before they cause failures.

quiz.q: What is a recommended self-insurance method for equipment repairs?
options: A) Set aside 10% of each gig fee
D) Buy new equipment each year
quiz.explanation: Setting aside 10% of gig fees creates a repair fund for emergencies.

quiz.q: How long do cables typically last before replacement?
quiz.explanation: Cables usually last about 2 years with regular use and proper care.

quiz.q: Why should you label equipment with your name and phone number?
options: A) To prevent theft or loss
quiz.explanation: Labelling helps recover lost items and deters theft.

quiz.q: How early should you leave for a gig 100km away?
quiz.explanation: Leaving 3 hours early accounts for bad roads and traffic delays.

quiz.q: What should you always carry with your equipment when travelling?
quiz.explanation: A checklist ensures you don't forget essential items.

quiz.q: How early should you arrive at a venue to set up?
quiz.explanation: Arriving 2 hours early allows time for setup and troubleshooting.

quiz.q: What document might you need for international gigs with equipment?
quiz.explanation: Passport, visa, and carnet are often required for international travel with gear.

quiz.q: What should you pack in an emergency kit for travel?
quiz.explanation: An emergency kit with water, snacks, painkillers, and clothes covers basic needs.

quiz.q: What is a good backup for power cuts during an event?
quiz.explanation: A generator or inverter provides reliable backup power for equipment.

quiz.q: What should you have as a backup for your main laptop?
quiz.explanation: A second laptop ensures you can continue if the main one fails.

quiz.q: What is a recommended cancellation policy?
options: B) Keep deposit if client cancels, refund if you cancel
quiz.explanation: This policy protects you from lost income while being fair to clients.

quiz.q: What should you do after a crisis at an event?
options: B) Review and update your plan
quiz.explanation: Reviewing the crisis helps improve your backup plans for the future.

quiz.q: Why is it important to stay calm during a crisis?
quiz.explanation: Staying calm reassures the client and helps you think clearly to solve the problem.
